items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water in plants.

rubric.why: Identifies the theory and its role in water movement through xylem.
rubric.description: States that cohesion and tension explain the movement of water through xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming cohesion and tension and linking them to water movement in xylem.

rubric.why: Explains how transpiration pull and cohesion move water upward.
rubric.description: Explains that transpiration creates tension and cohesion maintains a continuous water column that is pulled upward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining transpiration pull and the role of cohesion in maintaining the water column.

modelAnswer: The Cohesion-Tension Theory explains the upward movement of water through xylem in plants.
Transpiration from leaves creates tension, or a pulling force; cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous water column, which is pulled upward.

items.followUp: Name two structures found in eukaryotic cells but not in prokaryotic cells, and state their functions.

rubric.why: The presence or absence of a membrane-bound nucleus is a key difference.
rubric.description: Differentiates prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells by the nuclear membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that prokaryotes have no nuclear membrane while eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.

rubric.why: Membrane-bound organelles distinguish the two cell types.
rubric.description: Differentiates the cells by the presence of membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating that prokaryotes lack and eukaryotes contain membrane-bound organelles.

rubric.why: An additional valid comparison is required.
rubric.description: Gives a further accurate difference, such as relative size or genetic material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either the stated size comparison or the stated DNA/chromosome comparison.

rubric.why: The question requires a prokaryotic cell figure with identifying labels.
rubric.description: Draws a recognizable prokaryotic cell and labels its main structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognizable figure with the cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and nucleoid labelled.

rubric.why: The question also requires a eukaryotic cell figure with identifying labels.
rubric.description: Draws a recognizable eukaryotic cell and labels its main structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognizable figure with the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion and ribosomes labelled.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells have no nuclear membrane, whereas eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, whereas eukaryotes contain membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.
Prokaryotic cells are smaller than eukaryotic cells.
Draw a small oval prokaryotic cell and label cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and nucleoid.
Draw a larger eukaryotic cell and label plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion and ribosomes.

items.followUp: Describe how energy is released from ATP when it is converted into ADP.

rubric.why: Identifies ATP as the cell's energy currency.
rubric.description: Names ATP as the energy currency of the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ATP as the cell's energy currency.

rubric.why: Adenine and ribose are components of ATP.
rubric.description: Names adenine and ribose sugar as parts of ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both adenine and ribose.

rubric.description: States that ATP has three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the three phosphate groups.

rubric.why: The bond to the terminal phosphate is associated with energy release.
rubric.description: Identifies the high-energy bond involving the terminal phosphate group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the high-energy bond to the terminal phosphate.

rubric.why: ATP breakdown produces ADP and inorganic phosphate and releases energy.
rubric.description: States the products of ATP hydrolysis and that energy is released.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming ADP, inorganic phosphate and released energy.

modelAnswer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell.
An ATP molecule consists of adenine, a ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
The bond to the terminal phosphate group is a high-energy bond.
When this bond is broken by hydrolysis, ATP forms ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing energy for cellular activities.

items.followUp: Explain the role of source and sink in the transport of sugars through a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies where sugars enter the transport pathway.
rubric.description: States that leaves produce sugars by photosynthesis and act as a source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying leaves as the source where photosynthesis produces sugars.

rubric.why: Sugar loading into phloem sieve tubes is an essential step in the mechanism.
rubric.description: Explains that sucrose is actively loaded into phloem sieve tubes at the source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing active sucrose loading into the phloem sieve tubes.

rubric.why: Osmotic water entry raises pressure in the phloem.
rubric.description: Explains that water enters the phloem from xylem by osmosis, increasing pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the osmotic entry of water and resulting pressure increase.

rubric.why: The pressure difference drives phloem sap from source to sink.
rubric.description: Describes pressure-driven bulk flow from source to sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the pressure difference to bulk flow from source to sink.

rubric.why: Sugar unloading at sinks completes the transport pathway.
rubric.description: States that sugars are unloaded at sinks and used or stored, with water returning to xylem as an additional detail.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing sugar unloading at sinks and either its use or storage, or the return of water to xylem.

modelAnswer: Leaves are sources because they produce sugars, mainly sucrose, by photosynthesis.
Sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes of the phloem at the source.
The increased solute concentration draws water from the xylem into the phloem by osmosis, raising the pressure in the sieve tubes.
At sinks, such as roots, fruits or storage organs, sugars are unloaded and used or stored; pressure is lower there.
This pressure difference drives the bulk flow of phloem sap from source to sink; water can return to the xylem.
